extracted.intended_audience: readers of Gowers's weblog: mathematicians, math students and others able to read/evaluate elementary metric-space proofs (or willing to participate)
extracted.subtask_description: Collect qualitative and quantitative evaluations of short proof write-ups (here: three independent write-ups for five simple metric-space propositions). Participants should state their mathematical experience and give both comments and numeric ratings for clarity and style for each write-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description:
Rating scale for how easy the write-up is to understand:
-2 very hard to understand
-1 hard to understand
0 neither particularly hard nor particularly easy
1 easy to understand
2 very easy to understand
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate how understandable the argument is. Use this numeric scale for every write-up. Do not let this numeric rating substitute for written comments — both are requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style
rubrics_metrics.description:
Rating scale for the quality of writing/presentation:
-2 very badly written
-1 badly written
0 neither badly written nor well written
1 well written
2 very well written
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate the prose/notation/style choices of the write-up (wording, notation, flow). Use the same numeric scale for every write-up. Again, provide comments as well — ratings are not a substitute for textual feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: State mathematical experience level
rubrics_metrics.description: When participating, state your level of mathematical experience; the main thing requested is whether you have studied the basic theory of metric spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include enough information about background so the experimenter can interpret your ratings (e.g., 'no metric-space background', 'took metric/topology courses', 'graduate student in math', etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide comments and observations (qualitative feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants should make any comments/observations they wish on the write-ups; the post requests comparisons and preferences and emphasizes more detail is more useful (within reason).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete reasons for your clarity/style scores, note preferences between alternative write-ups, point out notational/flow issues or strengths, and be as specific as practical. The experimenter will moderate comments (initially hidden) and may publish them later unless you request otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rate every write-up independently
rubrics_metrics.description: Rate each of the 15 write-ups (three for each of five problems) for both clarity and style using the suggested scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each write-up separately and give two numeric scores per write-up (one for clarity, one for style). The write-ups' order was chosen randomly and independently; do not assume position encodes quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid influence from other participants' responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be influenced by the answers other people give; comments on the post go to the moderator's queue so participants won't see others' comments until data collection is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make your judgments independently so the experiment measures individual assessment rather than groupthink. If you don't want your comment published later, explicitly request that.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparisons and stated preferences between write-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimenter is particularly interested in comparisons and preferences between the different write-ups for the same proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, state which write-up you prefer for a given problem and why; note specific differences (e.g., notation choices, level of verbosity, use of pictures/open-ball language vs. epsilon-delta, naming conventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbosity of feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: The post asks for 'the more you say, the more useful it will be (within reason)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide substantive comments rather than only numeric scores; but avoid excessively long or off-topic remarks. Useful comments explain why a write-up is clear/unclear or well/poorly written and suggest concrete improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent interpretation of the rating scales
rubrics_metrics.description: So that everyone rates in the same way, the author suggests the above explicit numeric scales for clarity and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the provided labels when assigning numbers (e.g., don't treat 1 as 'neutral' if the scale defines 0 as neutral). Consistency across participants improves comparability of results.
